articles.title_orig: Pentagon offering military options to Trump as key midterm election deadline approaches
articles.title_zh: Pentagon offering military options to Trump as key midterm election deadline approaches
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — President Trump has alleged that elections, public benefit programs and federal grants to nonprofits are rife with fraud. Now, he is increasingly focusing on  fraud in his effort to detain and deport more immigrants.
Recent, high-profile flash points include 28 lawful permanent residents accused this week of illegally voting in California and the federal investigation into Somali-born Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).
The broader crusade takes many forms, including allegations of fraud in immigration applications , illegal voting by noncitizens and misuse of federal benefits by immigrants who don’t qualify.
“This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters,” said Royce Murray, a former senior official at the Department of Homeland Security under the Biden administration. That, she said, “serves a narrative that immigrants are not to be trusted and are here to take something rather than contribute, with an end goal of trying to make Americans less welcoming and more comfortable with a mass deportation agenda.”
On Tuesday, Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25-million program under the Justice Department to encourage the public to report suspected fraud in the U.S. government.
This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters
— Royce Murray, former Department of Homeland Security official
The White House said the first check, for $10,000, will go to right-wing influencer Nick Shirley, who posted a video last year alleging that Somali residents in Minnesota were running fake child-care centers to collect federal subsidies. Dozens of people were convicted in connection with a sprawling, $250-million children’s food assistance scheme that predated this administration, though more charges have been announced in recent months.
Also Tuesday, administration officials launched another nationwide anti-fraud crackdown, this time targeting immigrants who they allege have illegally collected SNAP benefits. Homeland Security highlighted the arrests of five people, calling them “the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation.”
“From day one of my administration, we’ve waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum,” Trump said during a news conference announcing the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program.
Earlier this year, the White House created a task force to eliminate fraud and the Department of Justice created a fraud enforcement division , in part, to target immigration-related offenses. Prosecutors have put aside thousands of other cases to zero in on immigration enforcement.
The focus on fraud has noticeably accelerated in the weeks leading up to the election.
Federal authorities charge 28 people in California with alleged illegal voter registration or voting, escalating the Trump administration’s fight with state election officials.
In California, some of the green card holders arrested this week over voter fraud said they didn’t remember registering to vote. The daughter of one defendant, Omar Muñoz, 72, of Belize, said she wondered whether her father had been confused with his U.S.-born son of the same name, who is a registered voter.
California officials pounced on the small number of people alleged to have cast illegal ballots. Illegal voting by immigrants “is so rare that the Trump admin is parading around town about .0001% of California voters,” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office wrote on X .
In the last seven weeks alone, the State Department said, 112 noncitizens across 20 states have been charged with illegal voting and registration offenses. Overall, since Trump returned to the White House, 155 people have been charged with voting fraud-related offenses.
Mullin and Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche said earlier this month that Homeland Security agents had secured 10 convictions and detained 100 others for civil immigration violations since August.
During the Biden administration, voter fraud charges were brought in just 13 cases, Blanche added.
Studies and audits of state voter rolls have repeatedly found that voting by noncitizens is rare and hasn’t swayed any elections.
Last week, with mail-in voting already underway, the Justice Department sued California , asking a federal court to bar the state from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters who were flagged by federal officials as “likely noncitizens.” Los Angeles County officials reviewed a sample of 200 of those voter registrations and found that nearly 40% indicated they were born in the U.S.
That number of flagged ballots — 20,000 — is a substantial reduction from the 190,000 noncitizens the administration alleged were on state voter rolls earlier this year, though federal authorities this week said they had found a “separate batch of 17,000 voting records potentially tied to noncitizens.”
California leaders pointed to other states , such as Nevada, where similar accusations have proved meritless.
Murray, the former Homeland Security  official, said she believes the administration is “trying to sow the seeds of doubt that the midterm outcomes will be trustworthy, so that if the Republican Party loses as badly as they’re predicted to, they can characterize it as due to fraud.”
Murray said the Trump administration has largely misconstrued what it means to commit fraud.
“Fraud is a very specific thing — it’s essentially lying,” she said. “Because you don’t get asylum does not mean you committed fraud, it just means you were ineligible.”
In September, a Homeland Security whistleblower told Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) that hundreds of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services employees had been tasked with quickly reviewing the voter information of thousands of people in search of suspected noncitizen voters, and were given a quota of investigating 40 subjects per day.
On Wednesday, a federal judge restricted Homeland Security agents from carrying out sweeping field operations aimed at rooting out voter fraud in nine states, including California.
It is against federal law for immigrants who are not naturalized citizens to vote or register to do so. Penalties can include fines, jail time and even deportation, though authorities rarely pursued that option.
Eric Balliet, a former special agent with Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, said he takes no issue with investigating fraud, but the timing of this operation and significant resources dedicated show it is “highly politically charged.”
Balliet worked for various administrations, including Trump’s first, before retiring in 2024.  Homeland Security Investigations agents typically focused on transnational criminal investigations such as drug smuggling and human trafficking.
Instead of initiating investigations based on tips or specific information, agents are now taking aggregated data and using algorithms to produce suspect lists, Balliet said. That’s not how law enforcement should operate, he said, calling it a massive privacy overreach against millions of law-abiding citizens.
“It’s the epitome of Big Brother,” he said.
Beyond the allegations of voter fraud, the Trump administration has also increasingly targeted immigrants on suspicion of lying to obtain a visa, green card or citizenship.
Omar’s family fled civil war in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S. in 1995 when she was 12. After agents searched her residence this month looking for evidence that her immigration paperwork contained falsehoods, she called the allegations baseless.

articles.title_orig: Apple's New iPhone Duo Breaks After 75,000 Folds in Real-Life Test
articles.title_zh: Apple's New iPhone Duo Breaks After 75,000 Folds in Real-Life Test
articles.content_orig:
Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, hit store shelves on Friday to considerable lines and long wait times for preorders.
But some customers who were lucky enough to get the $1,999-and-up phone on its first weekend have been reporting a pretty big problem: The inner screen of the phone can break, showing horizontal bright lines emanating from the phone's hinge.
Apple on Monday said that it was aware of the issue, which it said affected a "small number" of phones, and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty.
"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," an Apple representative told CNBC. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."
Apple says on its website that an inner-screen repair will be $999 for iPhone Duos that are out of warranty.
Most of the reports are from anonymous customers on online forums such as Reddit and X , and there are fake images online as well. But well-respected device repair firm iFixit weighed in on Sunday, after tearing down the new device and testing its resistance to dust, and theorized the issues may have to do with Apple's hinge design.
"Many of these damage reports describe folding or unfolding the phone, hearing a crunch, and pushing past it," said iFixit technician Shahram Mokhtari in its teardown video . "Right where the damage is happening, the hinge is shaped a little differently."
"The hinge is actually dozens of parts, with ludicrous precision," iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens posted on X. "A manufacturing variance or grain of sand can kill the fragile display panel it protects."
Breaking screens have been an issue with foldable phones going back to 2019, and have been seen as one of the major roadblocks to the technology's widespread adoption. That year, Samsung released one of its first folding devices, and reviewers quickly found that its inner screen cracked during normal use.
Early reviewers praised the experience of using the iPhone Duo when unfolded, especially for multitasking or media, but said that many apps had not been updated to take full advantage of the phone's larger and wider screens.
Apple said Monday that apps were already being updated for the new foldable device.
"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," an Apple representative said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia denies report that its CEO was allegedly targeted in Chinese spy plot
articles.title_zh: Nvidia denies report that its CEO was allegedly targeted in Chinese spy plot
articles.content_orig:
The report claimed the CEO was targeted by an executive at Megaspeed.
Nvidia, a top chipmaker, is denying a report that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was allegedly targeted in a Chinese spy plot.
According to a New York Times report published Thursday, U.S. intelligence officials allegedly determined that a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company who developed a "close relationship" with Huang was funneling information to Chinese officials in Beijing.
The executive was identified by the Times as Alice Huang, who was pictured together with the Nvidia CEO in 2024.
Nvidia denied the report in a statement to ABC News, saying Jensen Huang "talks with thousands of customer executives every year."
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected," the statement read. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job."
A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry also denied the report.
“The reports are baseless and purely slanderous smears against China,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Friday at his daily press briefing.
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment.
According to the Times, President Donald Trump was briefed on U.S. intelligence officials' findings but did not take any action.
The White House has not yet responded to ABC News' request for comment.
Trump is a close ally of Jensen Huang, who has advised the president amid an artificial intelligence race with China. Jensen Huang was a guest at a White House state dinner in September, where Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping.
That same month, the CEO attended a luncheon for AI and tech industry leaders hosted by Trump at the White House.
Earlier this year, in January, Huang convinced the president to clear the way for advance chip sales to China, in a deal that gave the U.S. government 25% of the profits.
Trump also personally owns shares in Nvidia, the world's most publicly traded company.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq hits near three-month low as Amazon, Intel rattle AI trade
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq hits near three-month low as Amazon, Intel rattle AI trade
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Sinéad Carew and Iain Withers
NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - A sharp selloff in Wall Street's tech shares pushed MSCI's global index down more than 1% on Friday, sending investors to the safety of US bonds on fears that hefty cash-burning AI investments ‌may not deliver sufficient returns.
Shares in chipmaker Intel plunged 28% and Amazon shares were off 1.9% after their results each showed they burned through ‌cash while investing heavily in AI-related development. Intel also said PC demand had slowed, and that it could persist through next year.
Shares in Google parent Alphabet, after falling 12.6% on Thursday, extended losses ​on Friday. Its massive AI spending turned the company cash flow negative while its search business faced stiff competition.
"It's really been a horror show this morning and the real villain is AI spending," said Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera, saying the heavy cash burn and elevated capex are prompting questions about whether the AI returns will "justify the outlays."
Goldman also said pressure from rising oil prices due to more attacks in the Middle East and concerns about a hack at Binance, the ‌world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, added to the gloom. Bitcoin ⁠and other cryptocurrency prices fell.
Outside tech, other sectors were holding up, particularly energy, which rose following results from Exxon Mobil and Chevron. The oil majors posted strong profits due to big refining margins driven by supply disruptions from Ukrainian attacks ⁠on Russian refineries and the US-Israel war on Iran. Shares rose 1.3% and 3%, respectively.
On Wall Street at 12:09 p.m. ET (1609 GMT), the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 384.61 points, or 0.73%, to 51,957.95, the S&P 500 fell 124.20 points, or 1.61%, to 7,595.93 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 684.06 points, or 2.61%, to 25,500.67.
MSCI's gauge of ​stocks ​across the globe fell 15.62 points, or 1.4%, to 1,117.00.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell ​0.46%.
In currencies, the yen headed for a third daily gain ‌on Friday after the Bank of Japan held rates steady but revised up its inflation forecast, while a fresh wave of selling in AI shares triggered demand for non-dollar safe havens.
The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.03% to 101.85, with the euro down 0.07% at $1.117.
Against the Japanese yen, the dollar weakened 0.2% to 157.37.
Bitcoin fell 1.80% to $77,424.37.
US Treasuries rose, putting benchmark 10-year yields on track for their biggest monthly decline since late 2023, as the tech-stock selloff pushed investors into safe havens.
The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 4.36 basis points ‌to 4.945% while the 30-year bond yield fell 0.69 basis points to 5.3221%.
The 2-year ​note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Federal Reserve, ​fell 5.4 basis points to 4.602%.
Oil prices were on track for a ​fourth straight monthly gain. Traders are bracing for a potential escalation in the US-Iran conflict after the US midterm elections. ‌The war has lingered for eight months without a resolution, and ​on Friday, a tanker in the Strait ​of Hormuz was attacked, highlighting the ongoing supply risks. [O/R]
US crude rose 2% to $104.09 a barrel and Brent rose to $117.58 per barrel, up 2.4% on the day.
Precious metals fell. Gold dropped to a one-year low on Friday and silver slid below $50 an ounce for the first time since ​November 2025 as higher energy prices and persistent inflation ‌concerns strengthened expectations that US interest rates will stay high.
Spot gold fell 3% to $3,901.83 an ounce. Spot silver fell 5.9% to $49.27 an ​ounce.
(Reporting by Sinéad Carew in New York, Iain Withers in London and Tom Westbrook and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore; Editing by ​Tom Hogue, Clarence Fernandez, Stephen Coates, William Maclean, Chizu Nomiyama and David Gaffen)

articles.title_orig: US scraps G20 photo after European diplomats object to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
articles.title_zh: US scraps G20 photo after European diplomats object to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
articles.content_orig:
European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in the US, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.
Two officials confirmed to the BBC the cancellation of the so-called family photo scheduled for Friday morning, which would usually include representatives from all the nations in attendance.
The meeting, which gathers top diplomats from the world's biggest economies, is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Ukraine is not not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.
Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is present and a diplomatic source confirmed the UK was among the countries which refused to participate in the picture.
One British official said: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".
A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".
"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.
In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

articles.title_orig: Tech stocks set to wipe out more than $1 trillion as concerns deepen about the AI boom
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks set to wipe out more than $1 trillion as concerns deepen about the AI boom
articles.content_orig:
Tech stocks plunged Friday, putting the Nasdaq 100 index on course for a more than $1 trillion drop. The index fell 3.4% in early afternoon trading, on course for its worst one-day drop since mid-June.
Driving the declines were shares of Amazon, which fell 3%, and Intel, which plunged 30%. Both companies reported quarterly earnings this week that failed to reassure investors and analysts.
Amazon had already lost as much as 10% late Thursday.
The broader S&P 500 also dropped sharply, by more than 1.7%. The index’s tech sector was by far the worst performing on Friday, tumbling more than 4.1%.
As trillion-dollar tech companies raise and spend hundreds of billions of dollars to build massive artificial intelligence data centers and develop AI models, investors have been on edge as they look for clear signs that all this spending is actually delivering returns.
On Thursday, Amazon reported that its spending to build out AI had continued at a faster clip than expected last quarter, while growth in its core online shopping business had slowed.
The last time Amazon told investors it was upping its AI spending budget, the market rewarded the decision by sending shares up more than 15%.
But a lot has changed in the past three months. Some of the big companies that pay to use AI models have tightened their token budgets. Others have raised questions about exactly how much benefit they’re getting from all the time and resources they’re putting into AI adoption.
In response, some investors are now looking at Big Tech’s massive AI spending through a more skeptical lens .
Nonetheless, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told shareholders Thursday to brace for even more spending.
“We still expect 2026 cash [capital expenditures] of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027,” he said on the company’s earnings call. Amazon’s spending had already been set to double from 2025.
Intel, meanwhile, told investors that its profits and sales in the fourth quarter would be lower than expected, which sent the stock tanking.
Friday’s losses follow significant selling in shares of Alphabet on Thursday .
The Google parent company shed about $500 billion in market value — its worst day ever and the second-worst wipeout of value in market history. On Friday, the stock dropped another 1%.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index, of which Intel is a member, sank 7.8% on Friday. Other major chip shares followed Intel lower.
The “DRAM” ETF, which tracks companies linked to computer memory and storage, tumbled 7.2%.
The Nasdaq Composite, which tracks every company traded on that exchange, fell 2.7%.
Intel’s stock has surged in recent months as its management implements a sweeping overhaul of the long-ailing chip firm.
In the midst of that turnaround, the U.S. government took a stake in the company , making the federal government the company’s largest shareholder.
Even accounting for Friday’s expected drop, the value of the government’s stake in Intel has grown by 280%.
Analysts at Citigroup described the report as “two steps forward, one step back.”
A major issue highlighted by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan that contributed to the company’s lackluster performance in the quarter was supply chain issues.
“I’m disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter,” Tan told investors on the company’s earnings call. “We face near-term challenges, including manufacturing, supply shortage, the unprecedented memory crunch and the resulting softness in PC demand.”
Meanwhile, the sell-off in tech shares appeared to increase demand for U.S. Treasuries, which briefly sent government bond yields lower.
The big AI companies that are borrowing hundreds of billions for data center build-outs have tapped the debt markets for funds, which has in turn created more competition for capital.
As those companies increasingly offer better rates of return for lenders than the U.S. government does on bonds, Treasury yields have risen in recent months — partly to keep up with the private market.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.title_zh: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.content_orig:
Marisa Liebana could barely hold back her tears as she sought news about her nephew Francisco Jose, one of the 69 victims of this week's high-speed rail crash in Spain.
Francisco Jose, 32, worked in Madrid and had caught a train south to the region of Andalusia on Wednesday to spend a few days with his parents. He was never seen again.
"The outcome has been very tough and very sad," Marisa said in the central city of Toledo, which has received most of the bodies from the collision outside the village of Urda.
"He was in the prime of his life," added Marisa, who said she felt "powerless" as she accompanied her brother Cecilio outside a reception centre for the victims' relatives in Toledo.
Inside the building, Civil Guard officers confirmed the dreaded news that their nephew had been found dead.
"We are devastated," Cecilio said, echoing the sentiment of the dozens of families affected by one of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century.
His sister, Francisco Jose's mother, could not come to Toledo. "She is distraught. She is seeing psychologists, receiving treatment, and she's in a really bad way," explained Marisa.
- 'Frustrated, outraged' -
Forensics teams are working around the clock and have identified 12 bodies, but for many relatives the wait is proving unbearable.
Esther San Emeterio, who is waiting for news of her brother Pepe, said the "anxiety" her family was experiencing was "crossing a line".
"Last night I went to bed incredibly frustrated, outraged, ashamed that no one is telling us anything."
Javier Barrio, whose wife Carmen de Santana had caught the train as one of her final work-related trips before her retirement, said "we are doing what we can, crying."
No DNA match or death certificate has been issued confirming her death, but Barrio is resigned to the worst, faced with the "extremely remote" chance of finding her alive.
"I've got my two children here who are supporting me a lot, but we're having a really hard time," he said.
Other families preferred not to speak as they paced up and down the area, overcome with shock, some with tears welling in their eyes.
Others found solace in an embrace with a loved one.
Ricardo, who is the friend of a family that suffered a bereavement, said the victim's parents had endured three days without knowing what had become of their child.
"And now he's in a body bag. It's incredibly harsh," said Ricardo.
- 'Scared' of train travel -
This week's accident is Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year -- a double blow to a network that had been a source of national pride.
Another collision between two trains in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people on the same line linking Madrid to the city of Seville.
"Who's going to get on a train now? Now you're scared when you do," said Cecilio, who wants such disasters to never happen again.
Spain was observing the second of three days of national mourning on Friday, with the public demanding answers just weeks before an early general election on November 29.
The right-wing opposition is already demanding the resignation of the transport minister and has lambasted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who is seeking re-election.
"Lots of lives have been lost in nine months. I think this should make everyone reflect -- the whole of society, the politicians -- about why this is happening in the 21st century," Cecilio said.
"I am not blaming one side or the other, but something is going wrong here."

articles.title_orig: Binance Hack Sends Crypto Stocks Tumbling
articles.title_zh: Binance Hack Sends Crypto Stocks Tumbling
articles.content_orig:
Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers.
On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea.
The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day.
By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital.
The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC.
"Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."
Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble.
In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data.
More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets.
What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.
Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted.
Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.
"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options."
GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin.
"Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC.
The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day.
Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment.
Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.
"Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment."

articles.content_orig:
The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to kill almost half of all those infected in that country, as the official case count now includes 10,141 confirmed cases, including 4,928 related deaths .
World Health Organization (WHO) officials say officials still record 50 to 80 new Ebola cases each day among eight affected DRC provinces, with 80% of cases coming from outside known transmission chains.
Genomic testing released today shows that recent cases in Nigeria and Kenya are from the same genetic group as current cases in DRC, but there is still no understanding of how the patient in Nigeria got infected.
The Nigerian patient visited Uganda from September 15 to October 3. The Kenyan index patient traveled from DRC through Uganda from October 1 to October 3. Both patients were at the Entebbe airport in Uganda on October 3. Both samples collected from the index patients do not carry any markers of the Ugandan Ebola cases reported in May and June of this year, eliminating the suggesting of underreported spread in that country. Instead, both carry the same genetic lineage as cases in the DRC.
Kenya has confirmed nine cases and two deaths, while no additional Ebola patients have been identified in Nigeria.
Although the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says Americans are at a low risk in the outbreak, the agency announced a new rule today stating all passengers boarding an international flight to the United States must attest via a signed statement that they have not been in the DRC during the previous 21 days.
The required attestation will begin on November 3 and last through December 18.
Travelers, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have been in DRC within 21 days before their flight will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations.
“Travelers, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have been in DRC within 21 days before their flight will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations and should plan to remain outside the United States for at least 21 days after they leave DRC,” the CDC said. “This includes all passengers transiting through DRC on a connecting flight regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane.”
The CDC said about 500 people at the agency are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries.
Today Director-General Jean Kaseya, MD, MPH, of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, warned that the Ebola outbreak could spread to the United Kingdom and other European countries.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said . “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.”
The CDC says drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause 9.7 million infections and 50,800 US deaths a year.
High levels of intestinal inflammation are linked to post-vaccination fever.
The state had not seen the disease in decades.
The gap between the diseases we fear and the actual dangers we face is significant. This Halloween, CIDRAP Director Michael Osterholm outlines the public health threats that worry him most.
Beginning November 3, international travelers to the US must attest they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo recently.
The second patient to die in Kenya was a close relative of the index patient.
But the University of Minnesota epidemiologist says the recognition belongs to a much larger group.
At the same time, confidence in the safety of longstanding vaccines, including MMR and polio, remains high.
The province has the world’s highest rates of the fatal neurodegenerative disease in animals such as deer, elk, and moose.
Pennsylvania remains the US hot spot, accounting for nearly 30% of the country’s cases.

ExxonMobil Profits Double to $15.4 Billion
Bloomberg reports that the EU…
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
ExxonMobil reported $15.4 billion in third-quarter profit Friday, more than double its earnings a year earlier, with its Gulf Coast refineries running at full capacity and diesel prices doing the rest.
The company earned $3.72 per share, or $4.23 on an adjusted basis, beating Wall Street's $4.08 estimate. Adjusted net income reached $17.5 billion, making it one of Exxon's most profitable quarters ever.
Exxon's energy products business earned $9.05 billion in adjusted profit, up from $4.1 billion in the second quarter. Its U.S. Gulf Coast refinery units operated at 100% utilization, producing their second-highest diesel volumes on record.
The Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have sidelined roughly 10% of global refining capacity, leaving the remaining plants to supply a market desperately short of diesel and other fuels. Refining margins have soared, and Exxon is certainly making the most of them.
The company has also increased the amount of fuel it can produce. Its Gulf Coast distillate output is up approximately 40% since 2019, helped by the $2 billion Beaumont refinery expansion completed in 2023. That project added 250,000 barrels per day of processing capacity, an investment approved years before today's fuel shortage.
Exxon's upstream business had a less impressive quarter. Adjusted earnings fell to $7.3 billion from $9.2 billion in the second quarter as crude prices eased. Production held near 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day.
Exxon generated $25.7 billion in operating cash flow and returned $9.4 billion to shareholders through dividends and stock repurchases, including $5.1 billion in buybacks. It also increased its dividend for the 44th consecutive year and announced plans for another $20 billion in share repurchases in 2027.
With Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries already operating at full capacity, further production increases will be difficult without additional investment. Global diesel supplies remain constrained by refinery damage in the Middle East and Russia, even as crude shipments from the Persian Gulf recover.

articles.title_orig: China expels record number of officials from CCP
articles.title_zh: China expels record number of officials from CCP
articles.content_orig:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

articles.title_orig: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.title_zh: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.content_orig:
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.
The Daily Express reported that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.
Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking , are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.
Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.
The Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.
Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage.
"All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries.
"We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.
At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.
Flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.
An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.
It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.
Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.
Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".
The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."
Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".
Jeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges.
Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.
Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.
In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office , in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.
Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.
Asked about the latest reports, Scottish First Minister John Swinney said: "I understand the seriousness of the points that have been made and the concern that has been expressed.
"This is an operational matter for Police Scotland to fully and comprehensively investigate and I'm very confident that's exactly what Police Scotland will do."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he did not want to comment on the police inquiries, which "should properly be independent".

articles.title_orig: Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year
articles.title_zh: Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year
articles.content_orig:
Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.
From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment.
Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds.
All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell.
"If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds'  Director of Insights Ivan Drury.
Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive .
And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive.
These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down.
There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place.
"I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve  until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data."
The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.
The Toyota RAV4 , which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand.
The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck.
The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani.
"We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said.
Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.
Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback.
"You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.
The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors ' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla.
The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990, and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000.
"Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."
Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars has risen and is up more than nearly any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used car market.
Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars.
Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly three in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost.
Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.
Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said.
The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said.
"It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."
Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said.
"The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to.  Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."
The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer.
"The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 is here, and alongside new features for Apple Photos , Messages , and Siri AI , the update also has a welcome addition for Find My: support for Apple TV 4K remotes.
Find My has long been the iPhone’s go-to hub for locating people as well as your Apple devices.
Except until now, there’s been one Apple device not included in the app.
The Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K has historically been absent from Find My. There was another way to locate it using the Remote app via Control Center, but most users probably didn’t realize that feature existed.
But with iOS 27.2, Apple TV remotes have now been added to the Find My app for location tracking. Open Find My in iOS 27.2 and go to the Devices tab, and compatible Siri Remotes (2nd gen and later) will now appear there.
It’s nice that Apple finally addressed this oversight, but the timing is no coincidence. That’s because the new Siri Remote (4th gen) is going to make finding a lost remote way easier.
The new remote features Precision Finding support and a built-in speaker . So the next time it’s lost somewhere in your house, your iPhone can direct you step-by-step to its location and trigger a noise to help.
The new Siri Remote is included with the 4th generation Apple TV 4K. But you can also buy it separately for $59 and get the same new features.
The upgraded remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models. To benefit from Precision Finding though, you’ll need an iPhone 17 or newer.
Did you know the Remote app offered support for finding a lost remote? Will you use the new feature in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on Trump military aid decision
articles.title_zh: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on Trump military aid decision
articles.content_orig:
A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.
Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.
Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.
The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".
Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.
"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.
On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".
Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.
Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.
Washington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.
US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.
In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.
Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.
Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".
It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".
Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.
Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.
Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.
"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.
"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.
US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.
The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.
The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.
He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.
"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.
"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."
He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

articles.title_orig: Three tankers strike mines and catch fire in Strait of Hormuz, Iran claims, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Three tankers strike mines and catch fire in Strait of Hormuz, Iran claims, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Iran said four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis claimed missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating pressure on two fronts as the U.S. reportedly weighs renewed military action against Tehran after Tuesday's midterm elections.
The flare-up is fueling concern among regional officials and analysts that fighting could resume around the Nov. 3 vote, even as Vice President JD Vance seeks to reopen talks with Iran.
The developments underscore the competing diplomatic and military tracks now shaping the conflict, which now in its ninth month.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three tankers caught fire after striking mines along what it called an "unauthorized southern route" near the Omani coast. Iran's army said a fourth burned east of the strait.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a small boat attaching two explosive devices to a tanker about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. The blasts sparked an engine-room fire that disabled the vessel, the agency said, adding that the crew was safe.
Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Thursday also challenged a U.S. Central Command statement that American forces had cleared mines from the primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway carried about one-fifth of the world's energy supplies, and has seen traffic plummet to single-digit daily passings since the war started in late February.
"Prove the claim that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of mines with independent evidence, not a statement," IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said. "The reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the air, on land and at sea, not on social media and in America's media war rooms."
Iran-backed Houthi forces said they launched six military operations across Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil facilities, despite a rare meeting of Saudi and Iranian senior officials in Tehran earlier this week. The two sides had agreed to resolve regional differences through dialogue.
Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attacks but said their air defenses have intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone launched toward the holy Mecca region.
Earlier this week, Vance sent a letter via Qatari mediators to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, proposing a framework for talks.
President Donald Trump, when asked whether he directed the outreach, said "no," framing it as Iran needing " help with medical supplies and various things ." "He [Vance] asked me what I thought. I said, 'if you want to do that, that's OK,'" Trump said.
Reports have emerged that the Trump administration may resume military actions in the Middle East after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Adm. Brad Cooper, top U.S. commander in the region briefed Trump on military options for Iran in a rare in-person visit to the White House, the Wall Street Journal reported late Thursday, citing unnamed U.S. officials close to the matter.
The meeting, joined by other cabinet members, covered other topics including the continuing U.S. blockade, according to the report.

articles.title_orig: Spanish minister refuses to resign over second major train crash on his watch
articles.title_zh: Spanish minister refuses to resign over second major train crash on his watch
articles.content_orig:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s deadly train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.
Sánchez said the Spanish state was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding that his government was committed to finding what had caused Spain’s second deadly train collision this year.
Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am . After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear , knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
“ It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.
“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system.
Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken ; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”
Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente – who is under growing pressure to resign – gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.
“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “ The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”
Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but stressed that such incidents were not at all uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers ultimately reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .

Bulgaria’s next president will be elected in a runoff vote on Sunday, after a close race between the two main contenders ended inconclusively in the first round.
The incumbent Iliana Yotova , former vice-president to Bulgaria’s former president and current prime minister Rumen Radev , faces pro-European opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov.
The two candidates will pit contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarised contest on Sunday, AP noted.
Contrary to pre-election expectations by observers for a double-digit difference in favour of Yotova, her opponent showed a surprisingly strong performance coming just 2.8 percentage points behind her and leaving all options open for the runoff.
AP noted that Bulgarians vote against a backdrop of growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping, which have left several sailors dead or missing.
Polls will open 7am local time and close 8pm local time.
The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it is closing, citing pressure from authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor and earlier this year detained one of its journalists.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” the editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, said in a video statement published on YouTube on Friday. “The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Russia has introduced near-Soviet levels of censorship since sending troops to Ukraine, pushing the vast majority of independent journalists into exile. Novaya Gazeta, a bastion of independent journalism in Russia, is classed by Moscow as a “foreign agent”, a label used to stifle dissent.
Sokolov said: “ Novaya Gazeta has been killed … On 9 November we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
This month Sokolov was taken in for questioning and Russian authorities searched his home over a criminal case involving one of his colleagues, Oleg Roldugin, who was arrested in April.
Russia has intensified its crackdown on independent news outlets since its offensive on Ukraine in February 2022. Novaya Gazeta cut down production inside Russia after the offensive began. Authorities revoked its media licence the same year.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel peace prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.
In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”.

articles.title_orig: Review: Predator Atlas 8: Is Arc G3 Extreme a Game-Changer for PC Handhelds?
articles.title_zh: Review: Predator Atlas 8: Is Arc G3 Extreme a Game-Changer for PC Handhelds?
articles.content_orig:
Acer's $1300 / £1300 Predator Atlas 8 is here, one of a handful of new PC handhelds to launch this year despite crippling price rises to components like RAM and SSDs. The special sauce here is Intel's first handheld-specific chipset, the Arc G3 Extreme. Does the new hardware move the needle compared to existing AMD Z2 Extreme handhelds like the ROG Xbox Ally X20 ? And how does Acer's handheld compare to better-known rivals like Valve, Asus and MSI in terms of design?
Before we get into the performance testing, it's worth quickly running through the design of Atlas 8. It's a chunky, handsome device in a pleasant dark grey chassis, and I like the colours chosen for the face buttons. However, it does feel a step behind rivals like the Xbox Ally X when it comes ergonomics, with quite geometrically basic grips and a robust 810g weight - significantly heavier than a 640g Steam Deck or 540g Switch 2.
The sticks and triggers use modern TMR sensors, which is great for longevity and precision, but the circular d-pad leaves a little to be desired and the buzzy, off-putting vibration makes it feel like you're holding a horrendous metallic wasp - some distance away from the more detailed and restrained Microsoft-derived Xbox Ally devices when it comes to vibration.
The eight-inch 1920x1200 120Hz VRR screen is thankfully a lot more competitive. It's no OLED when it comes to contrast and colour reproduction, but it gets bright enough for outdoor use, provides wide viewing angles and doesn't exhibit any distracting ghosting or other artefacts, so fast motion looks good. Overall, it's a better offering than the Switch 2's LCD, but a step behind the Steam Deck OLED - and with the powerful Arc G3 Extreme chipset on board, the handheld has the genuine capability of reaching high frame-rate territory for a change. The prominent speakers flanking the bottom of the screen are also amongst the loudest I've ever heard on a handheld, and I spent most of my time with the volume at around 10 percent as a result.
When it comes to performance, Intel's Arc G3 Extreme is a massive step beyond the AMD Z2 Extreme chipset that powers the Xbox Ally X.
The Atlas 8 was able to outperform the Xbox Ally X by around 50 to 70 percent at matched settings at a rated TDP of 35W, albeit with the Xbox Ally X using FSR 4 - which carries a small performance penalty, often around 5 percent. Generally speaking, this brought average sub-60fps games on the Xbox Ally X into the 80s and 90s, allowing extra headroom for increasing settings or simply a more responsive experience that takes better advantage of the 120Hz display.
The Atlas 8 offers four options - a 25W quiet mode, 30W balanced mode and 35W turbo mode, while a manual setting allows you to bump up the total to 40W - though its jargon-filled warning ("Changing PL1/PL2 may cause system instability") needs rewriting in plain English.
I only had the Atlas 8 for around four days of testing, so I focused my attention on five games with built-in benchmarks at 35W on both machines: Civilization 7 (CPU and GPU), F1 25: 2026 Season Edition, Forza Horizon 6, Returnal and Red Dead Redemption 2. The full results, including game settings, are shown below.

While the Atlas 8 performs incredibly well, even the brief testing experience I had was held back by a litany of bugs and poor design decisions in Windows 11. Despite improvements to the Xbox launcher and better usability for gamepad controls, the initial setup experience is torturously long and asks many irrelevant questions for a gaming handheld; driver and software updates are spread amongst nearly half a dozen different places; and at several points applications crashed or simply stopped working, necessitating a restart. I'm hesitant to blame Acer for any of these problems, as I experienced many similar issues on the Xbox Ally X, which has been on the market for considerably longer.
To take just one example, I wanted to install GPU driver updates before testing. New drivers weren't available via Windows Update, nor were they offered in the Intel Arc Control app. I eventually used Edge to visit the Intel Driver and Support Assistant page, which required a separate download and install. Once this was finished, the page had a generic error message, which I needed to fix by clicking on the lock icon next to the URL in Edge, setting the "apps on device" setting to enabled, and reloading the page. This was frustrating enough as a long-time user of Windows and Windows handhelds, so I can't imagine what it would be like for a relative newcomer. On SteamOS, by contrast, this would have been sorted with a simple trip to the Settings menu to install the latest updates.
Other issues I experienced in just a few days with the device included some Steam games missing from the Xbox launcher, Windows Firewall messages still popping up in the year of our lord 2026, the handheld's lights and fans remaining on while the screen and buttons stop working, games missing from the alt-tab and Xbox switcher menus while running, Explorer not responding to touch inputs, and taking nearly two hours to reset Windows 11 back to stock after testing while I waited, already long overdue in bed.
As Rich says in the X20 review : "This didn't feel like any kind of console experience - because too much of standard Windows intrudes and in that sense, it still feels off-putting."
It's much the same on the Atlas 8, and that's a shame. Perhaps the likes of SteamOS, Bazzite and other handheld-focused Linux distributions could give these handhelds a better user experience, but expect driver compatibility to be an issue at least in the short to medium term. For now, the expectation is that these are Windows 11 devices, and that means accepting some level of usability compromises versus Steam Deck or Switch 2.
Despite the rough edges that persist in Windows, the $1300 / £1300 Atlas 8 is still a great handheld that is well worth considering. The surfeit of performance available here brings a new generation of games into handheld playability, even if Intel's XeSS has fallen a little behind the latest generations of DLSS and FSR. The design work here is also solid, with some ergonomic improvements and weight saving to find in later iterations, but fundamentally there's nothing here that prevents the Atlas 8 from becoming your primary gaming device on the go.
The new Acer handheld is about to be released in the US - Best Buy shows a November 2nd release date - and I'm fascinated to read more reviews from critics and users alike once the handheld is available for a wider audience. For example, I'd be interested to see more in-depth testing of performance and battery life when gaming in quiet mode. As always, individual reviews are necessarily limited in scope, so I encourage you to read widely to get a balanced view.
