articles.title_orig: Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures
articles.title_zh: Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures
articles.content_orig:
Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures
Saturday is Warhammer Day ! It’s also Halloween, so, to get ready we’re taking a look at some of our favourite terrifying Warhammer miniatures.
Their whispered war cry is the last thing you’ll hear. These living suits of armour can’t be reasoned with, can’t be stopped, and they’re armed with magic guns!
Once proud Space Marines, Rubric Marines are now nothing more than a pile of dust and a corrupted soul, trapped inside a suit of power armour for all time, and commanded like a puppet by the arcane magic of warp-fuelled sorcerers. Some fates are worse than death.
What would Halloween be without vampires? Blood Angels may not dislike garlic, but they are incredibly stylish, and do crave the taste of blood. Just remember, Space Marines have two hearts, so you’d better bring two stakes!
Blood Angels have a second flaw – the Black Rage – and none have ever truly been able to overcome it. That was until Mephiston , Chief Librarian of the Blood Angels, crossed the Rubicon Primaris and seemingly left his curse behind him. Don’t think he won’t nibble your neck though.
While they may look skeletal, there’s no organic matter to be found on a Necron Warrior . These deathless automatons march without fear or mercy in eerie lockstep with a single-minded desire to destroy every living creature in the galaxy. You may be faster, but they’ll chase you forever.
Necron Warriors form the undead legions of the dynasties, and if it wasn’t scary enough staring into their dead, soulless eyes, then their guns can flay the flesh from any living creature. On top of that, one of their star gods was death incarnate, and is said to be the inspiration for the grim reaper .
The Nighthaunt are no mere ghosts, they are bitter, ethereal spirits that inflict terror, and drag down the souls of the living. Not to put too fine a point on it, these are not kids wearing bedsheets with eyeholes cut into them.
No figure in the worlds of Warhammer embodies the misery of the restless undead more than Lady Olynder, Mortarch of Grief . She is despair made manifest, gloom given form, and mortals in her presence are overwhelmed by a dread so potent that it can silence the heartbeat of even the strongest opponent.
While the motley assortment of creatures that make up the Gloomspite Gitz may seem “fun” to the casual observer, make no mistake, Squigs have very sharp teeth. And a lot of them.
When grots take to the battlefield with a horde of Squigs , woe betide anyone who underestimates these vicious creatures. Little more than mouths with legs and a terrible appetite, Squigs are feared across the Mortal Realms, able to tear even the mightiest foe to shreds in a crimson blur.
The full moon shines down through the inky black darkness. Out on the moor, you hear a blood-curdling howl. Wulfen are part Space Marine and part wolf, and they are probably the closest thing to a werewolf in the 41st Millennium.
Wulfen are bestial warriors, altered by the curse lying in the gene-seed of all scions of the Wolf King – hunters that bound forward with fangs bared and claws outstretched. They’re fast, and they hit hard with claws, teeth, and a variety of deadly weapons.
Join us in-store to celebrate Warhammer Day and Halloween! You’ll be able to pick up other scary models, such as skeletons , zombies , and other undead warriors . Plus, you can get Oath Fulfilled , the special commemorative miniature, who, if she gets sufficiently blessed by the Dark Gods, might make it onto this list for next year.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol: 'The turn has occurred' — now it's in growth mode
articles.title_zh: Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol: 'The turn has occurred' — now it's in growth mode
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations.
However, its U.S. turnaround continues to take hold, as its home market topped expectations during the coffee giant's final quarter of fiscal 2026.
"We enter fiscal 2027 with momentum, a clear set of priorities and higher ambitions for what Starbucks can become," CEO Brian Niccol said in a video shared on the company's website.
Starbucks is ahead of schedule to meet the fiscal 2028 targets laid out at its investor day in January, he said on the company's earnings conference call.
For fiscal 2027, Starbucks is projecting adjusted earnings per share in a range of $3.15 to $3.25, above Wall Street's expectations of earnings per share of $3.14. However, its anticipated revenue decline of 1% is weaker than expected; analysts were forecasting net sales growth of 1.4%.
Starbucks is projecting North American same-store sales growth of 4% for the fiscal year.
The company's earnings and revenue outlook includes an additional week and the effects of the shift in its China business to a joint venture business model. Starbucks is also projecting slight deflation in coffee prices and slowing net new North American cafe openings, which will both weigh on its full-year revenue, according to CFO Cathy Smith.
Here's what the company reported for the quarter ended Sept. 27 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Starbucks reported fiscal fourth-quarter net income attributable to the company of $677.2 million, or 59 cents per share, up from $133.1 million, or 12 cents per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring and impairment costs and other items, the company reported earnings per share of 80 cents.
Net revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, reflecting the joint venture deal in China.
The company's global same-store sales increased 7.2%, fueled by growth in average ticket, and beating Wall Street estimates of 6%, according to StreetAccount. Transactions grew 1.8% in the quarter.
Starbucks' U.S. cafes reported same-store sales growth of 7.7%, topping StreetAccount estimates of a 6.5% increase.
Under Niccol's "Back to Starbucks" strategy, the company has focused on improving service, making its cafes more welcoming and sharpening its marketing. The changes have helped to win back customers.
"Starbucks brand affinity is at near record levels as our menu innovation, marketing and merchandise continue to create moments that drive culture and bring people into our coffee houses," Niccol told analysts.
The company said its North American rollout of its fall menu, which includes the iconic pumpkin spice latte, was the company's strongest ever autumn launch day. And matcha is now a $1 billion drink for Starbucks.
Outside of North America, the company's international comparable sales ticked up 0.9%, as traffic declines offset an increase to average ticket. That growth fell short of analyst estimates of a 3.2% increase, according to StreetAccount.
After its China business transitioned to a joint venture, Starbucks has shifted most of its international business to a licensed model, allowing local operators to take charge. The company is also exploring selling a majority stake in its Japan business, Reuters reported in September.
Starbucks opened 303 net new cafes during the quarter. In September, the company announced it would close about 1% of its North American footprint, or about 250 locations, as part of its turnaround.
By the end of its fiscal year, across the U.S. and Canada, the company also completed more than 1,700 cafe uplifts, meant to make its stores more welcoming to customers. The company has said locations that receive a makeover, with tweaks like increased seating and softer lighting, see higher transactions in the aftermath.

articles.title_orig: Putin open to phone call with Zelensky, Ukraine suspects a Kremlin trap
articles.title_zh: Putin open to phone call with Zelensky, Ukraine suspects a Kremlin trap
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin is seeking to avoid a face-to-face meeting between President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin by proposing they speak by phone instead, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
The apparent move comes as Kyiv insists the two leaders should meet in person to address the most pressing issues in negotiations , including Russia's territorial demands and security guarantees. Such a meeting would be their first since 2019.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Oct. 30 that Putin was "open to dialogue with everyone." Asked whether the Russian leader would speak with Zelensky by phone, Peskov added that "no one has called yet."
The comments came as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, which Kyiv sees as a possible starting point for a meeting between the countries' leaders.
Ukrainian officials privately suspect Moscow is trying to arrange a phone call that they believe would achieve little while avoiding the prospect of a face-to-face meeting.
"They've already tried to do this over the phone," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Kyiv has long pushed for a direct meeting between Zelensky and Putin.
The two leaders last met in person in Paris in December 2019 during the Normandy Format talks mediated by France and Germany. They have not held direct talks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine has made several attempts to arrange a meeting since then.
Zelensky invited Putin to Istanbul for talks on May 16, 2025, proposing a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump to advance peace efforts. Putin declined to attend and instead sent a delegation led by a low-level presidential aide, Vladimir Medinsky.
After meeting Putin in Alaska in August 2025, the U.S. president said he was working to arrange a meeting between the Russian and Ukrainian leaders.
Trump later said Putin was reluctant to meet Zelensky because "he doesn't like him."
Now, every time the Ukrainian side raises the idea of a meeting at the level of leaders, the Kremlin challenges the Ukrainian president to come to Moscow for it. Zelensky has called for Putin to meet him in a neutral location.
Kyiv continues to argue that only direct talks between the leaders can produce meaningful decisions on the most difficult issues. Ukrainian officials say the Russian representatives sent to negotiations do not have the authority to make such decisions.
"Territorial issues can only be discussed by the leaders of the countries at war, and only at their level," Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 27. "No one else has the authority to do so."
Territory remains one of the main obstacles to an agreement.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the parts of Ukrainian Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts that Russian forces have failed to capture. The strategically important regions in eastern Ukraine remain central to the negotiations.
Ukraine, by contrast, has called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
Several people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent that Washington supports the idea of a leaders' meeting and that Trump could help arrange one.
The G20 summit in Miami in December could serve as a possible venue, the people said. Under this scenario, if Putin accepts Trump's invitation to attend, Zelensky could also travel there to meet the Russian leader.
As Ukraine pushes for a meeting, its officials believe Moscow is trying to undermine the effort by offering alternatives that would not require Putin to meet Zelensky.
One senior Ukrainian official questioned whether a phone call could resolve the issues at stake without U.S. involvement.
"Well, what do we want? To reach a final decision on key issues and security guarantees ," the official told the Kyiv Independent. "Is it possible to do this over the phone — and only over the phone — without the U.S.? No."
"We need a trilateral format with the U.S., plus some involvement from the Europeans ... But they're like, 'Well, just go to Moscow ,' or call us, but what good will a phone call do?"
Ukrainian officials fear that Moscow's insistence on a phone call could give it another reason to walk away from negotiations without making meaningful commitments. They argue a meeting with third parties would better address the disputes.
Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. plan to hold talks in Abu Dhabi in November, focusing on steps to de-escalate the war. Moscow has signaled readiness to resume negotiations with Kyiv after a pause of more than eight months.
Zelensky said the planned technical talks should seek concrete progress on de-escalation, including an energy and maritime ceasefire, prisoner exchanges , and discussions about a possible trilateral meeting between the leaders.
"We hope for a result regarding energy and at sea, an exchange of prisoners, and a discussion of the possible format for a trilateral meeting at the leaders' level."
Kyiv does not expect working-level negotiations alone to end the war.
Ukrainian officials say Putin must take part in the process himself if the talks are to produce actual decisions.
"Putin needs to come out of his bunker and take part in the trilateral talks," the senior Ukrainian official said. "And personally confirm that he is ending the war."
Tim Zadorozhnyy is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering foreign policy, U.S.-Ukraine relations, and political developments across Europe and Russia. He studied International Relations and European Studies at Lazarski University and Coventry University. Tim began his journalism career in Odesa in 2022 as a reporter for a local television channel. He later spent a year and a half at the Belarusian independent media outlet NEXTA, first as a news anchor and later as a managing editor. He is fluent in English, Ukrainian, and Russian.

articles.title_orig: What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
articles.title_zh: What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
articles.content_orig:
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.
Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government.
The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53.
Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population.
"Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran."
The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect.
The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power.
Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister.
The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear.
"An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement.
The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."
Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters.
Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."
While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins.
Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results.
"Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post.
Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on —   Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.
Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically , will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
T-Mobile (TMUS) declared a $1.17 quarterly dividend representing a 14.7% raise, but the stock has fallen 26% year to date, which has artificially inflated today's 3.2% yield.
I bonds pay 4.26% with inflation protection and state-tax exemption but limit purchases to $10,000 per year and lock up cash for 12 months.
Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and T-Mobile didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat TMUS. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.
Series I savings bonds carry a 4.26% composite rate on bonds issued from May 1, 2026 through October 31, 2026. That window closes this week, and a new rate applies to bonds issued starting November 1, 2026. On the stock side, T-Mobile ( NASDAQ:TMUS ) traded at $146.32 in premarket trading on October 28, 2026. Against its annualized forward dividend of $4.68 per share, that works out to an indicated yield of about 3.2%. Neither number is a guaranteed return, and they differ in more ways than the rate.
An I bond is a savings bond sold directly by the U.S. Treasury. Its rate has two parts. The first is a fixed rate , currently 0.9%. It stays with the bond for its full life. The second is a semiannual inflation rate , currently 1.67%. It tracks inflation and resets every six months. Treasury combines the two with its own formula to produce the composite rate. The inflation component is never locked. It can fall as easily as it can rise, and each bond's rate changes every six months from its issue date.
The rules are strict, and they matter to anyone who may need the cash:

Why Didn't TMUS Make The Top 10 List?
24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now . Not the ten biggest companies. Not the ten everyone is arguing about. The ten best stocks to buy right now.
And TMUS didn't make the cut!

Enter Your Email and See the Ten →
Purchase cap: electronic purchases are limited to $10,000 per person per year.
Lockup: you cannot cash the bond for the first 12 months.
Early-redemption penalty: cash it before five years and you give up the last three months of interest.
Maturity: the bond earns interest for 30 years, then ends. Your original investment plus all accrued interest is paid to you at redemption.
Interest is added to the bond's value instead of being paid out as cash. Anyone who needs a quarterly check must redeem the bond to get it.
Start with whether the payment holds up. T-Mobile's dividend has grown fast. It paid $0.65 per share per quarter through 2024, $0.88 in 2025, and $1.02 starting in late 2025. On September 24, 2026, the board declared a $1.17 per share dividend, a 14.7% increase. It goes ex-dividend on November 25, 2026, and pays on December 10, 2026.
Cash flow covers it well. Management raised full-year 2026 adjusted free cash flow guidance to between $18.4 billion and $18.8 billion, with cash capex of about $10 billion. Second-quarter free cash flow was $4.797 billion. The board's 2026 shareholder return authorization of up to $18.2 billion covers both buybacks and dividends, and buybacks are the flexible piece. Since the program began in Q3 2022, T-Mobile has returned $44.2 billion through buybacks and $10.4 billion through dividends.
Those strains are real, though. Total debt excluding tower obligations stood at $86.9 billion as of Q2 2026. Postpaid churn rose to 0.99%, and costs from the UScellular merger and the retail overhaul are still running through results. The CFO said the company is maintaining a capital budget for spectrum auctions in 2027 and 2028, which will compete with cash for shareholder returns.
Investors have noticed. The stock is down 26.35% year-to-date and 31.91% over the past year. Telecom shares also slid after reports that SpaceX had held cell tower talks for Starlink Mobile (Forbes). Much of today's yield comes from that falling price, not from a fatter payout.
Here is the core tradeoff. A Treasury-backed I bond cannot have its payment cut by a board, and its redemption value never falls. It also cannot grow beyond what the fixed rate and the inflation formula deliver. A T-Mobile dividend can grow, as it has every year since it started, and it still has room to grow. It can also be cut, and the shares behind it can lose value. The stock's 11.55% drop over the past month shows how quickly that can happen.
I bonds carry risks of their own. The government guarantee covers your principal and accrued interest. It does not cover your purchasing power beyond what the formula captures, and it does not let you buy more than the annual cap. The biggest risk is reinvestment risk : if inflation cools, the variable component resets lower, and the composite rate falls with it, while the 0.9% fixed portion stays put. Money is also tied up for a year, and you give up interest if you redeem early.
The federal government taxes I bond interest as ordinary income. It is exempt from state and local taxes. Cash-method taxpayers can also defer the federal tax until the earlier of the year you cash or dispose of the bonds or the year in which they mature. That lets a retiree choose the year the income shows up, ideally a low-income year. Interest may also be excluded under the Education Savings Bond Program if you redeem bonds in the same year you pay qualified higher education expenses, such as a grandchild's tuition, subject to that program's rules.
T-Mobile's dividends count as qualified dividends if you meet the holding-period test. Federal law treats qualified dividend income as net capital gain under 26 U.S.C. § 1(h)(11), so it is taxed at the preferential rates for long-held assets, which are usually lower than ordinary income rates. Dividends are taxable at the state level, and you owe tax in the year you receive them, with no option to defer. The I bond's state exemption helps where state taxes are high. In a no-income-tax state, the lower federal rate on dividends may count for more.
I bonds suit retirees who want inflation-linked savings that can never lose value, who can leave the money alone for at least a year (ideally five), and who live in a high-tax state or want to choose when interest becomes taxable. T-Mobile's dividend fits income investors who want quarterly cash today and a payout with a record of growth, and who can ride out share-price declines like this year's. Before relying on that payout, they should be comfortable with the company's debt load and its spectrum spending plans. articles.title_orig: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.title_zh: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.content_orig:
It’s a good time to be an oil company.
The two largest U.S. oil companies, ExxonMobil and Chevron, on Friday reported blowout profits that easily beat expectations as oil prices remain sharply elevated because of the U.S. war with Iran.
ExxonMobil reported a profit that doubled from the same period last year, while Chevron’s earnings surged more than 180% from a year earlier.
As part of the bumper returns, Exxon said it was increasing the dividend it pays to investors.
The returns at both companies came as the price of oil surged beyond $100 per barrel and has remained there for months. On Friday, prices accelerated again, with Brent oil trading just under $118 per barrel.
The highest level that Brent reached since the United States and Israel launched the Iran war in late February was $126, which it is now approaching again.
Since the start of the year, Exxon shares have risen 52%, and Chevron shares have returned 50%.
Overnight, another major oil company, BP, reported that its profit skyrocketed to an 18-year high.
The average price of regular gasoline has soared 40% for consumers since the war broke out. Soaring prices continue to pressure consumers ahead of the midterm elections, where voters have repeatedly said that prices and inflation are primary concerns.
In 2024, Donald Trump repeatedly pledged to drive energy costs down . “My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office,” the then-candidate said in September 2024, while adding that it would mean “gasoline below $2 a gallon.”
As of Friday, the average gasoline price is currently more than double that.
In recent rallies on the campaign trail, the president has celebrated the higher oil and gas profits. “I wonder if I should say this,” Trump mused aloud during a rally Oct. 24, before saying “our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East.”
Trump touts U.S. oil business making ‘hundreds of billions’
“My people said, ‘Please don’t mention that, sir,’ because people are paying a little higher,” Trump continued. “But what we’ve done for this country, we’re making money like this country has never made before.”
“I don’t give a damn: I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.”
The higher prices are also a result of the war between Ukraine and Russia following President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of his neighbor in 2022.
“There’s a lot of disruption happening in the world,” ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday morning . “What you’re finding is because of the closure” in the Strait of Hormuz, “shipping has to find new routes around to continue to deliver the products that society desperately needs.”
“About half of Russia’s refinery capacity has been taken out from the Ukraine bombing,” he added.
“That shortage of refining capacity and availability to the world is what’s driving product prices as high as it is, and frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth,” Woods continued.
Since the start of the year, the average nationwide price for diesel fuel has risen 78%. New York-traded diesel futures have soared 130% since the start of the year, likely indicating more price rises could still come at the pump.
Both Exxon and Chevron said that they were running their refineries at maximum output to continue making as much diesel as possible.
Trump has taken specific note of the impact that diesel could have on the economy. The administration has quickly issued multiple orders and policies in an attempt to bring prices down.
The president signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road dyed variety of diesel, has pressured European allies to release more of the diesel reserves into the global market, and has announced a deal with Putin for some of that country’s diesel supplies.
Trump’s latest move came last week, when he announced $150 million in Defense Production Act funding to “expand petroleum production, storage, and logistics at refineries across.”
The moves have not meaningfully brought prices down.
On Friday, Woods said his refineries were already being pushed to the limit. “We are at record levels of utilization for our refineries,” he said on CNBC.
“If you look at North America, we produce record volumes of diesel. That’s all been a function of trying to drive more product into the marketplace to meet that demand and to drive costs down.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

Companies like Hoto and Fanttik have elevated the design and functionality of tools like electric screwdrivers , but Arrowmax wants to make them smarter by adding a camera and AI that work together to eliminate the trial and error of finding the exact type and size of bit you need. It’s convenient, but also helpful, as choosing the wrong size could potentially leave you with a stripped screw and a much harder repair.
Arrowmax is making the Arrowspace S1 available through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign , but the company has already successfully crowdfunded other products. You can preorder the screwdriver by itself for around $79, but its functionality and usefulness is expanded by bundling it with the S1 smart bit case that bumps the preorder price to around $129. Full retail pricing will be higher, and the S1 isn’t expected to ship until April 2027 at the earliest.
On the bottom of the S1 is a small camera with an LED light that’s used to capture an image of a screw head. To ensure the screwdriver’s AI model has the best possible image to work with, next to the camera is a “precision contact probe” that extends and rests on the surface of the screw to ensure the camera is always at the ideal focus distance.
Once the AI processes the photo, the type and size of bit you need will be displayed through a connected mobile app. Based on the identified screw, the screwdriver will also automatically select a safe torque setting to reduce the risk of damaging the fastener. To save you the trouble of having to find the exact bit that’s needed, the optional S1 Smart Case has a collection of 52 steel bits with an LED next to each one that lights up so the one you need is easy to spot.
The Arrowspace S1 features a 600mAh rechargeable battery the company claims delivers enough power to run for up to 90 minutes, or tighten or loosen over 900 screws. That performance will vary if you turn off the automatic torque adjustments and increase it yourself. The remaining charge is displayed on the screwdriver’s OLED screen which also shows the current torque setting and which direction it’s set to rotate.

articles.title_orig: Google Stock Plunges 12% on AI Fears, but Joseph Carlson Isn't Selling, Says Shares Look Cheap
articles.title_zh: Google Stock Plunges 12% on AI Fears, but Joseph Carlson Isn't Selling, Says Shares Look Cheap
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Google’s parent company tumbled more than 12% on Thursday, their worst day on record — a historic single-day decline bigger than any day during the Covid-19 pandemic or 2008 financial crisis.
The drop erased roughly half a trillion dollars in Alphabet’s ( GOOGL ) market value, the second-largest single-day wipeout in history, after Nvidia’s nearly-$600 billion slide in early 2025 .
Investors are increasingly scrutinizing Big Tech’s AI spending spree and how the technology is affecting their own businesses — and Alphabet is their latest target.
The company’s shares dropped sharply as investors fretted over slowing growth in Google’s search advertising business occurring alongside a continued ramp-up in spending on AI.
The world’s largest technology companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build data centers, in a race to try and be among the winners of the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street is getting more cautious, attempting to sort out which companies are spending rationally, how those outlays are impacting other parts of their business, and who will actually benefit from AI’s transformative impact on society.
Alphabet reported quarterly sales figures on Wednesday that missed analysts’ expectations. Investors were dismayed by the miss in sales figures, which reignited longstanding concerns about whether the company’s cash cow — Google’s search advertising business — will be able to withstand the pressure of consumers increasingly using Google’s own (and competitors’) AI chat bots in the place of traditional search.
The fear is that this displacement might happen “faster than Google can react to it and pivot their business,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management.
The company also disclosed a second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow, another metric causing concern among investors. Since going public in 2004, Google — which became Alphabet in 2015 — hadn’t posted a single quarter of negative free cash flow until this year. Strong free cash flow is one sign of a healthy company that can pay dividends, conduct share buybacks and reinvest in its business.
Alphabet recorded $51.4 billion in capital expenditures in the third quarter alone, compared to $91.4 billion for the entire year in 2025. As the company ramps up its spending on AI, including data center construction, it’s leaving less cash for the kind of immediate gratification investors love, like share buybacks and dividends.
In stark contrast to Alphabet’s negative free cash flow, Microsoft reported this week that it had $18.6 billion in free cash flow in the third quarter, even as it continues to spend billions on its AI buildout. Microsoft’s shares ended the day flat on Thursday while Alphabet shares dropped more than 12%.
“We are now getting to see who is spending rationally on AI and who is not,” said Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners.
It might seem odd that shares of one of Big Tech’s biggest companies aren’t soaring after Anthropic filed its highly anticipated initial public offering prospectus just days earlier. Anthropic is committing to spending a lot of money to rent compute power from tech companies like Alphabet.
But that future promise isn’t guaranteed, especially if the data center buildout doesn’t go to plan or if AI isn’t as profitable as expected. Alphabet is asking investors to believe in its vision for AI and the data center buildout, while also trying to monetize AI and show it can generate strong returns from the technology.
Growth in Big Tech companies’ cloud computing divisions is a sign that demand for AI continues to be robust. But the market is on edge about anything that could go wrong for the AI boom.
Big Tech companies like Alphabet are turning to debt and financial markets to raise more capital to help fuel their ambitions. While companies say they are trying to keep up with demand, the competition for funds from investors is rising.
“Everybody is trying to get through the door at the same time, and it gives people pause,” said Ted Mortonson, an investment strategist at Baird who focuses on the tech sector.
Wall Street is becoming more disconcerting about the data center buildout, and companies that are burning through free cash flow are getting punished.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu's bloc falls short as longtime allies reportedly weigh move that could end his rule
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu's bloc falls short as longtime allies reportedly weigh move that could end his rule
articles.content_orig:
With final election results leaving both major blocs short of a majority, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Israel on the negotiations that could determine the country's next government.
Israel's final election count has confirmed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has lost its parliamentary majority, but whether opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot can assemble a government to replace him remains an open question as negotiations begin behind closed doors.
The completed count, published early Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee , gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition alliance. The two predominantly Arab parties secured a historic 19 seats, placing them in a potentially decisive position.
Netanyahu's Likud emerged as the largest individual party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad with 12. Final voter turnout reached 77.9%, according to the Central Elections Committee results .
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW
Posters of former Israeli Chief of General Staff and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot, right, and Prime Minister and Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu are seen as election campaigns intensify two days before the vote as campaign posters of candidates are displayed on billboards and buildings across the streets ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for October 27, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
But the numbers leave neither major bloc with the 61 seats required for a majority, opening a complex political struggle involving potential partnerships with Arab parties, ultra-Orthodox lawmakers or a unity government bringing together longtime rivals.
A source familiar with opposition discussions, who spoke to Fox News Digital on condition of anonymity, described the outcome as a "bitter stalemate," but not an impossible political situation.
The source said opposition leaders are approaching coalition negotiations with patience and experience rather than treating the inconclusive results as a defeat, arguing that the next government could depend on their ability to forge partnerships that previously seemed unlikely.
FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER
An ultra-Orthodox Jewish man holds his ballot as he votes in the parliamentary election at a polling station in Jerusalem on January 22, 2013. Israelis voted on Tuesday in an election widely expected to win Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a third term in office, pushing the Jewish State further to the right, away from peace with Palestinians and towards a showdown with Iran. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
In a potentially significant development Friday, Israeli journalist Yishai Cohen of Kikar HaShabbat reported that Rabbi Dov Lando, a leading ultra-Orthodox religious authority, had instructed lawmakers from Degel HaTorah, part of United Torah Judaism, to open discussions with the opposition.
According to the report, the objective is to reach an arrangement protecting the status of yeshiva students amid the longstanding dispute over mandatory military service.
Channel 12 reported that figures within the ultra-Orthodox party were considering allowing an Eisenkot-led minority government to survive through outside parliamentary support, potentially breaking with Netanyahu.
"Our votes are not in Netanyahu's pocket," party figures told Channel 12, according to a translation of the Hebrew-language report.
However, the office of United Torah Judaism Chairman Yaakov Asher denied that any instruction to begin negotiations had been issued.
Such an arrangement would represent a significant shift from the party's longstanding alliance with Netanyahu. Eisenkot's pledge to expand military conscription among ultra-Orthodox men remains a major obstacle, although Channel 12 reported that party figures were willing to consider a compromise on the issue.
The source familiar with opposition discussions told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot's camp had been preparing for the possibility of cooperation with ultra-Orthodox parties well before the election, suggesting that some of the options now being discussed had already been under consideration behind the scenes.
According to the source, such an arrangement could require compromises over military service and potentially outside parliamentary support from Arab lawmakers, bringing together political factions whose positions appeared irreconcilable during the campaign.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, on October 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Another possibility rests with the Arab parties, which nearly doubled their parliamentary representation from 10 to 19 seats following a surge in turnout.
But the prospects of an Arab-backed government have drawn conflicting assessments.
Channel 12 reported Thursday that Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas had expressed deep skepticism about the possibility of establishing an Eisenkot-led minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.
Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also argued that the available options had narrowed considerably, identifying a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government or another election as the two principal remaining possibilities.
Mohammed Majadla, head of the news division at Radio Nas and a Channel 12 political commentator, offered a different assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital, arguing that both Ra'am and the Joint List were prepared to use their parliamentary influence to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.
"The two Arab lists agree on two things," Majadla said in the Hebrew-language interview. "First, they are prepared to do everything within the political process to ensure Netanyahu does not return to power."
According to Majadla, that could include joining a coalition, providing outside parliamentary support or abstaining from key votes.
He said their second shared priority was avoiding another election, which Arab political leaders fear could reverse their gains.
"The ball is now in Eisenkot's court, not in the Arab parties' court," Majadla said. "As far as the Arab parties are concerned, I can tell you they are truly prepared to do everything to make this happen."
Majadla suggested that public declarations should not necessarily be treated as final positions, particularly as parties seek leverage during coalition negotiations.
The difficulties extend beyond the Arab parties. Eisenkot's potential partners include politicians who strongly oppose cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, while several opposition leaders campaigned against relying on Arab lawmakers to govern.
NETANYAHU FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL FUTURE AS ISRAEL HEADS TO POLLS WITH IRAN THREAT LOOMING
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, of the Likud Party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar Party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026. Israel heads to the polls on October 27 in its first election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, in what is seen as a referendum on the prime minister. (Jack Guez / AFP via Getty Images)
A national unity government involving Likud and Yashar would offer a more straightforward mathematical route to a majority, but would require Eisenkot to reconsider his campaign pledge not to join a Netanyahu-led government.

articles.title_zh: North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach
articles.content_orig:

Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance . The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.
The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change.
In a post on X , Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto.
The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains.
Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”
Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”
It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices.
Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.
Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds.
Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.
Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.”
Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .
According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes.
Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million .
The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction.

articles.title_orig: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
articles.title_zh: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
articles.content_orig:
(FOX 2) - General Motors will pay $220 million to settle allegations it sold customers' private data that eventually ended up in the hands of insurance companies.
The behavioral data was then used by the industry to set insurance rates for consumers.
Michigan will receive more than $7 million in the settlement, the attorney general said on Thursday.
A coalition made up of more than half the states in the U.S. were part of a class-action lawsuit against the Detroit automaker after millions of drivers enrolled in GM's Smart Driver program had their driving habits tracked then sold to third party companies.
The program was intended as a tool by GM to help drivers improve their own safety. They also told drivers their data would not be shared. It took place from 2016 to 2024.
Instead, the information was sold to data brokers "under contracts that specified the data was to be used for insurance products," a release from the Michigan Attorney General said.
Some drivers saw their premiums rise based on their driving habit data being obtained by insurance companies.
Attorney General Dana Nessel's office said most of the customers who signed up for the Smart Driver program when they bought a GM at a dealership and that employees had accepted the terms of the program on behalf of the customers without their consent.
GM's own system also failed to let drivers know their data was being tracked, including through its OnStar app, which inaccurately told 370,000 drivers they were not enrolled in the tracking program even though they were.
"GM later quietly unenrolled these drivers without telling them about the mistake and allegedly left their data with the data brokers and insurance companies," Nessel's office said.
The states involved in the suit include: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Florida, Hawai’i, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin.
GM issued a statement after the settlement was announced:
"This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices. Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share."
The Source: The Michigan Attorney General was cited for this story.

articles.title_orig: 'Bad time to troll': Binance cofounder Changpeng Zhao asks Elon Musk for 'respect' after post about bitcoin hack
articles.title_zh: 'Bad time to troll': Binance cofounder Changpeng Zhao asks Elon Musk for 'respect' after post about bitcoin hack
articles.content_orig:
The cofounder and former CEO of Binance asked Elon Musk not to "troll" the company on Friday and instead "show some support" after the SpaceX CEO appeared to mock the embattled cryptocurrency exchange in a series of social media posts.
After learning the world's largest crypto exchange had been hit by a $6.3 billion hack late Thursday, Musk posted several emojis, ranging from laughing to grimacing, on X.
In response, Changpeng Zhao reminded the SpaceX and Tesla CEO of Binance's equity stake in Musk's businesses.
Binance’s SpaceX stake, which stems from an earlier investment in what was then-Twitter, is worth more than $1 billion, Zhao said.
That's a tiny fraction of SpaceX's roughly $2 trillion valuation.
"Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop," Zhao wrote. "Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!"
It's not the first time the pair has sparred online.
In Nov. 2021, Binance suspended Dogecoin withdrawals because of a wallet glitch, a measure Musk called "shady". In reply, Zhao highlighted a major Tesla recall of almost 12,000 U.S. vehicles due to software glitches and hardware issues.
Binance froze all withdrawals and deposits after the hack, which investigators suspect to be the work of North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor. It has since restored deposits.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far.

articles.content_orig:
Italy has tightened security as tens of thousands of students and unions took to the streets across the country.
Marches were held in dozens of cities nationwide on Friday. Rome, Milan and Naples were among those affected by the protests, which targeted soaring living costs , demanded investment in education and called for an end to the wars in the Middle East.
A large police presence was on hand, as the hard-right government tightened security measures in a bid to control potential unrest seen in Italy and other European states in recent weeks.
In Rome, security was stepped up around the Colosseum, Italy’s most visited tourist attraction, while Milan’s cathedral also received special protection.
A few skirmishes between protesters and riot police occurred at the start of a protest in Turin, with other rallies in Bologna and Genoa.
The USB trade union called for a general strike that attracted large numbers of demonstrators, including truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers. Rallies in recent weeks have demanded an end to higher fuel prices and rising defence spending.
Unions have also issued a joint call with peers in France, Greece, Spain, Turkiye and Morocco to demand an end to the wars in the Middle East, including the war in Gaza and “an end to the militarisation of ports”.
“Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,” the statement said. “Dockworkers do not work for war!”
The government last week agreed on a 175 million euro ($195 million) aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.
The prices paid in Italy for food, energy, transport and bills have risen by 68 percent since 2000, while the average wage fell by almost 5 percent.
Measures to support young people and families – such as an annual bonus of 2,500 euros for workers under 30 – have also been inserted into the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties.
“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general… who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said at a news conference on Wednesday, stressing that the measures were “not for those who smash windows”.
Following clashes over the weekend of October 17-18 between youth and police in Milan, in which groups of mainly young people looted shops and smashed windows, Meloni toughened laws on public gatherings and eased restrictions on the detention of minors.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu isn’t acting like he won the election. Here’s what that could mean
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu isn’t acting like he won the election. Here’s what that could mean
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s right-wing bloc won 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset, results released by election officials Thursday showed, well below the 68 it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament.
The bloc supporting Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot , won 48 seats in an extremely tight race , meaning neither secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday.
Herzog will then consult with party chairs and choose a candidate ⁠he thinks has the best chance to form a government.
Parties led by Israel’s Arab minority made historic gains, winning a combined 19 seats in a race in which Palestinians with Israeli citizenship headed to the polls in record numbers Tuesday, many hoping to oust Netanyahu and far-right members of his coalition, including Bezalel Smotrich, his finance minister, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Both leading blocs have ruled out the possibility of forming a government with the two main Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List. But their rise as potential kingmakers has brought the complex realities faced by Palestinian Israeli nationals into fresh focus.
Ahead of the election, Netanyahu and other members of his coalition amplified allegations of foreign election interference , referring Arab parties to the domestic security service, the Shin Bet, for investigation over allegations of Qatari intervention.
Qatar denied the allegations. Mansour Abbas, the head of Ra’am, said his party had “no connection” to such conduct and urged a full investigation. He also accused Netanyahu of a “campaign of incitement and delegitimization ” against Arab citizens.
Dean Livne, the acting director general of Israel’s Central Elections Committee, said in a published letter sent to a member of parliament that there was “no basis for allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity.”
Before the election, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties.
But Yair Golan, the head of the smaller left-wing Democrats party, called for a government formed “in partnership” with Arab parties. “We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said Wednesday on X.
The majority of Palestinians with Israeli citizenship are the descendants of those who remained within what became Israel during the war that led to the country’s founding in 1948. At the time, hundreds of thousands more fled or were expelled from their homes. Palestinians refer to this as the “ Nakba ,” which means “catastrophe” in Arabic.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event
articles.title_zh: UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event
articles.content_orig:
Andreas Malm said he had been notified by the Home Office that he would not be allowed into the UK
A Swedish climate academic says he has been barred from entering the UK because he was due to speak on a panel with a co-founder of Palestine Action.
Andreas Malm told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had received a letter from the Home Office notifying him that his presence was "not conducive to the public good", with no further details given.
He said he could not "see any other explanation" for being denied entry than his scheduled appearance with Huda Ammori, a founder of the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.
The Home Office said it did not comment on individual cases.
Malm is a senior lecturer in human ecology at Sweden's Lund University, whose work includes the 2021 book How to Blow up a Pipeline and 2025's The Destruction of Palestine is the Destruction of the Earth.
He said he had asked the Home Office to explain its decision, but could not see a reason beyond the upcoming talk in London with Ammori organised by the left-wing magazine Tribune - calling the move a "severe restriction on the free exchange of ideas".
Malm said he was not a member of Palestine Action, had never publicly endorsed it, nor had he given it any financial support.
"The only link to Palestine Action is her as a person," he said, criticising the UK government for ascribing "guilt by association".
The academic acknowledged that he had previously described the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel - in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage - as "fundamentally an act of liberation".
Malm said it was possible that these remarks, during a December 2023 talk in which he also condemned the "deplorable" killing of civilians in the cross-border attack, had been the reason for the Home Office's decision.
But he argued that these views had been in the public realm for a long time, including when he was last allowed into the UK to deliver a talk in May.
"I don't expect the British state to agree with me on Palestine or climate or anything. What I expect the British state to do is to continue to let me enter the country and to discuss with colleagues, with people who disagree with me - as I have done for years."
Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's controversial ban under terrorism legislation . The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of the group. About 2,500 have been charged, though none have gone to trial as the legal challenge to the proscription continues.
The government has broad discretion to bar foreign nationals from entering the UK if their presence is deemed to pose a risk to society.
In April, 11 people described by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer as "far-right agitators" were banned from entering the UK ahead of a rally led by Tommy Robinson.
Kanye West was also denied entry that same month after backlash to his planned set at London's Wireless Festival, following a string of antisemitic, racist and pro-Nazi comments. He had previously apologised for the remarks and said his bipolar disorder had caused him to lose "touch with reality".
Left-wing political commentators Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur claimed in June that their visas had been revoked ahead of planned appearances in London and Oxford, allegedly "for criticising Israel" .

articles.title_orig: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
articles.title_zh: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
articles.content_orig:
FILE - The Binance logo is seen on a smartphone, Feb. 28, 2023, in Marple Township, Pa. Matt Slocum/AP hide caption
A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.
The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.
The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."
TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.
Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.
Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

articles.title_orig: Beijing drills water cannons and drones near disputed South China Sea shoals
articles.title_zh: Beijing drills water cannons and drones near disputed South China Sea shoals
articles.content_orig:
Training off Second Thomas and Sabina shoals tests small boats, surveillance drones and simulated vessel boardings amid ongoing spats
China’s coastguard has carried out an exercise featuring water cannons and drones near two disputed reefs at the centre of its simmering South China Sea contention with the Philippines to prepare for “foreign infringement”, according to state media.
A China Coast Guard flotilla “recently” conducted “comprehensive maritime law-enforcement training” in the waters around Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal, according to state broadcaster CCTV, which did not specify dates.
The official television network stated that the drill had focused on foreign vessels “illegally” entering the waters around the two shoals, while covering surveillance, tracking, maritime traffic control and tactical manoeuvres by small boats.
It also included practising water cannon use, drone operations and optoelectronic evidence collection – a technique that uses optical and electronic sensors to detect and record evidence that may not be visible to the naked eye – according to the report.

articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s bloc loses parliamentary majority, Justice Department subpoenas California officials
articles.content_orig:
As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.
Israel's final election count has confirmed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has lost its parliamentary majority, but whether opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot can assemble a government to replace him remains an open question as negotiations begin behind closed doors.
The completed count, published early Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee , gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition alliance. The two predominantly Arab parties secured a historic 19 seats, placing them in a potentially decisive position.
Netanyahu's Likud emerged as the largest individual party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad with 12. Final voter turnout reached 77.9%, according to the Central Elections Committee results .
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW
Posters of former Israeli Chief of General Staff and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot, right, and Prime Minister and Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu are seen as election campaigns intensify two days before the vote as campaign posters of candidates are displayed on billboards and buildings across the streets ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for October 27, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
But the numbers leave neither major bloc with the 61 seats required for a majority, opening a complex political struggle involving potential partnerships with Arab parties, ultra-Orthodox lawmakers or a unity government bringing together longtime rivals.
A source familiar with opposition discussions, who spoke to Fox News Digital on condition of anonymity, described the outcome as a "bitter stalemate," but not an impossible political situation.
The source said opposition leaders are approaching coalition negotiations with patience and experience rather than treating the inconclusive results as a defeat, arguing that the next government could depend on their ability to forge partnerships that previously seemed unlikely.
FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER
An ultra-Orthodox Jewish man holds his ballot as he votes in the parliamentary election at a polling station in Jerusalem on January 22, 2013. Israelis voted on Tuesday in an election widely expected to win Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a third term in office, pushing the Jewish State further to the right, away from peace with Palestinians and towards a showdown with Iran. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
In a potentially significant development Friday, Israeli journalist Yishai Cohen of Kikar HaShabbat reported that Rabbi Dov Lando, a leading ultra-Orthodox religious authority, had instructed lawmakers from Degel HaTorah, part of United Torah Judaism, to open discussions with the opposition.
According to the report, the objective is to reach an arrangement protecting the status of yeshiva students amid the longstanding dispute over mandatory military service.
Channel 12 reported that figures within the ultra-Orthodox party were considering allowing an Eisenkot-led minority government to survive through outside parliamentary support, potentially breaking with Netanyahu.
"Our votes are not in Netanyahu's pocket," party figures told Channel 12, according to a translation of the Hebrew-language report.
However, the office of United Torah Judaism Chairman Yaakov Asher denied that any instruction to begin negotiations had been issued.
Such an arrangement would represent a significant shift from the party's longstanding alliance with Netanyahu. Eisenkot's pledge to expand military conscription among ultra-Orthodox men remains a major obstacle, although Channel 12 reported that party figures were willing to consider a compromise on the issue.
The source familiar with opposition discussions told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot's camp had been preparing for the possibility of cooperation with ultra-Orthodox parties well before the election, suggesting that some of the options now being discussed had already been under consideration behind the scenes.
According to the source, such an arrangement could require compromises over military service and potentially outside parliamentary support from Arab lawmakers, bringing together political factions whose positions appeared irreconcilable during the campaign.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, on October 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Another possibility rests with the Arab parties, which nearly doubled their parliamentary representation from 10 to 19 seats following a surge in turnout.
But the prospects of an Arab-backed government have drawn conflicting assessments.
Channel 12 reported Thursday that Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas had expressed deep skepticism about the possibility of establishing an Eisenkot-led minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.
Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also argued that the available options had narrowed considerably, identifying a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government or another election as the two principal remaining possibilities.
Mohammed Majadla, head of the news division at Radio Nas and a Channel 12 political commentator, offered a different assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital, arguing that both Ra'am and the Joint List were prepared to use their parliamentary influence to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.
"The two Arab lists agree on two things," Majadla said in the Hebrew-language interview. "First, they are prepared to do everything within the political process to ensure Netanyahu does not return to power."
According to Majadla, that could include joining a coalition, providing outside parliamentary support or abstaining from key votes.
He said their second shared priority was avoiding another election, which Arab political leaders fear could reverse their gains.
"The ball is now in Eisenkot's court, not in the Arab parties' court," Majadla said. "As far as the Arab parties are concerned, I can tell you they are truly prepared to do everything to make this happen."
Majadla suggested that public declarations should not necessarily be treated as final positions, particularly as parties seek leverage during coalition negotiations.
The difficulties extend beyond the Arab parties. Eisenkot's potential partners include politicians who strongly oppose cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, while several opposition leaders campaigned against relying on Arab lawmakers to govern.
NETANYAHU FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL FUTURE AS ISRAEL HEADS TO POLLS WITH IRAN THREAT LOOMING
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, of the Likud Party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar Party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026. Israel heads to the polls on October 27 in its first election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, in what is seen as a referendum on the prime minister. (Jack Guez / AFP via Getty Images)
A national unity government involving Likud and Yashar would offer a more straightforward mathematical route to a majority, but would require Eisenkot to reconsider his campaign pledge not to join a Netanyahu-led government.
For Netanyahu, the lengthy coalition formation process could provide additional opportunities. If Eisenkot receives the mandate to form a government but fails, President Isaac Herzog could assign the task to another candidate, potentially giving Netanyahu another chance to assemble a coalition. articles.title_orig: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.content_orig:
The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds.
The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.”
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.
“ This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said.
As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value.
Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them.
Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X .
Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement.
The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.
Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million . Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead.
Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .
David Ingram is a tech reporter for NBC News.
